newsitem.title: USA: Congress' recess may hold up Midwest disaster aid.
newsitem.headline: Congress' recess may hold up Midwest disaster aid.

text.p: Congress appeared ready Thursday to go home for its week-long Memorial Day recess without passing an emergency bill providing $5.5 billion for the flooded Midwest and other weather-ravaged states.
Despite days of talks, Congress and the White House could not bridge their differences on spending and environmental provisions that had drawn veto threats from President Clinton.

Republican leaders Thursday afternoon were also backing away from Plan B -- an effort to pass a slimmed-down bill providing $1 billion in disaster relief, nutrition aid for poor women and children, and U.S. peacekeeping operations.
"The wisdom of the age is 'do nothing,'" said a frustrated Bob Livingston, the House Appropriations Committee chairman who had struggled to convince Republican leaders to move the small bill.

Livingston was concerned some states would run short of relief money if Congress refused to act. Lawmakers from more than 30 states that would have received funds under the bill did not want to go home to voters empty-handed.
Aides said top Republicans were concerned they would lose leverage in future negotiations with the White House if some of the must-pass aid was stripped out.
Congress is set to recess Friday. But aides said that even though the small bill appeared dead, last-minute resurrection was possible.
Democrats blamed the Republicans for the impasse, accusing them of burying the bill under a pile of unrelated amendments.

"For my Republican colleagues to consider going away for Memorial Day when these people are waiting for their flood relief money ... is disgraceful," Massachusetts Democratic Representative Joe Moakley said.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle, whose state was hit by harsh weather, condemned the lack of action on a bill.
"I don't know if there's anything more important. I believe it's even more important than the (balanced) budget agreement this week," he told reporters.
Lawmakers still hope to finish work on the overall $8.4 billion disaster aid bill when they return from their break.

The legislation contains $5.5 billion to aid more than 30 states hit by floods, mudslides and harsh weather. It provides about $2 billion for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and continued military flights in the Gulf.
One big hurdle is a provision that would automatically keep the government open next year if Congress and the White House failed to agree on needed spending bills.

Clinton has threatened a veto over that plan, arguing that it would provide billions less for domestic spending than allowed under the new balanced budget deal. The White House also said the plan would reduce pressure to compromise on spending issues.

Republican leaders are eager to avoid a repeat of two unpopular government shutdowns during fiscal 1996, which voters blamed on their party. They profess amazement that Clinton would be willing to risk another shutdown.
The White House further opposes a proposal by Ted Stevens, chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, to make it easier to build roads on federal lands in Alaska.
The administration said the Alaska Republican's plan could allow roads in pristine areas. Stevens argues that Western states need better transportation systems.

Another big dispute is over a plan to bar the government from spending money on sampling or other statistical techniques for the 2000 census. The administration says sampling could provide a more accurate count of minorities.
